# Serving and Memory Principles {.unnumbered}

Part III analyzes the systems infrastructure required to serve stateful, multi-turn agent trajectories at scale. We treat the context window as an active L1 attention working set, develop Radix-tree prefix caching to eliminate redundant prefill compute, address the tool-wait idle memory crisis via hierarchical KV-cache paging over PCIe/CXL, and design trajectory schedulers for heavy-tailed workloads.

::: {#pri-vol3-attention-working-set .callout-principle title="Context as an L1 Working Set"}

**Invariant**: Context capacity is the L1 cache of neural compute: expressive, fast, strictly finite, and quadratically expensive in compute ($O(C_i^2)$) and linear in HBM capacity.

**Implication**: Runtimes must actively manage context via eviction and semantic compaction to prevent Time-To-First-Token (TTFT) explosion and attention degradation.

:::

::: {#pri-vol3-prefix-coherence .callout-principle title="Prefix Locality and Coherence"}

**Invariant**: Multi-turn agent trajectories exhibit massive prefix sharing; serving runtimes must exploit Radix-tree KV reuse while maintaining strict cache coherence when environments mutate.

**Implication**: Prompts must be engineered with static prefixes first, and serving schedulers must route multi-turn turns with session cache affinity.

:::

::: {#pri-vol3-heavy-tailed-scheduling .callout-principle title="Trajectory-Aware Scheduling"}

**Invariant**: Agent workloads exhibit heavy-tailed Pareto service times and bimodal latency structures that break classical request-level queueing models.

**Implication**: Cluster schedulers must combine predictive admission control, cache-affinity routing, and preemption policies constrained by the Reversibility Boundary.

:::
